media.title: How Much Surface Does It Cover?
media.context: This hook opens the first topic, straight after the chapter opener. Students have no method. The film must not compare the two patches and must not mention unit squares as the answer.
media.description: A rangoli is filled with powder, then a tiled floor and a wheat field flash past, and two odd shaped patches sit side by side. Which one covers more surface? The eye cannot settle it.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Recognise area as the amount of surface a shape covers. Key teaching points: 1) Area measures the surface inside a boundary. 2) The eye cannot compare irregular shapes reliably. 3) A common unit is needed for comparison. 4) Counting equal squares gives that unit. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often compare shapes by their longest dimension. 2) Students often judge area by how tall a shape looks. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of two odd patches: ask which patch the class thinks is bigger. 0:25, just before the open question: ask what they would need to be sure. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what area is measuring. After viewing, ask how they would compare two odd shapes.

topics.summary: A square can be split into four equal-area parts in infinitely many ways. Reshaping a part by squeezing one edge and stretching the opposite edge by the same amount leaves its area untouched.

content.text: The area of a region is the number of unit squares it covers. If you make a piece shorter along one edge but longer along another edge by the matching amount, the product of the two edges stays the same, so the piece still covers the same number of unit squares. This is why a square can be cut into four equal parts in endlessly many ways: as long as the parts share the whole equally, each one keeps its quarter of the area no matter how it is reshaped. Cutting a figure into pieces and rearranging them into a new figure of the same area is called dissection.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Rectangles, squares and the meaning of area
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what stays fixed when a region is reshaped through observation and reasoning, and determine that shortening a piece along one edge while lengthening it by the matching amount along another keeps the product of the edges the same, so the count of unit squares it covers never changes. They will explain that a square of side 8 covers 64 unit squares and splits into four parts of 16 each in endlessly many ways, since every rearranged piece still holds its quarter of the area.

media.title: Rectangle Area Array
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Area (Mensuration). The rectangle formula is PRODUCED from the tiling rather than announced, which is why the tool is placed where the formula is first stated. It carries the Class-6 counting convention forward — area is the count of unit squares, written in square units — and then deliberately breaks the OTHER Class-6 rule the student brings with them: the estimate convention for irregular figures on squared paper (ignore a part under half, count a part over half as a whole). Here nothing is ever rounded, because a rectangle has a formula and the formula is exact. Vocabulary follows the Indian textbook: length and BREADTH, l × b, rows of unit squares, square units.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the exact area and the array that counts it.
whatYouLearned: Area is the number of unit squares a shape covers, and it is written in square units
A rectangle holds equal rows of squares, so length times width counts them all at once
Adding the sides measures the boundary, not the surface
Half unit sides give part squares that combine, so the formula stays exact

overview.goal: The student computes a rectangle's area by rows and columns, explains why multiplication counts them, and extends the argument to fractional sides.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying one rectangle laid on squared paper, the way a tiled floor is looked at from directly above. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class splits over whether covering a rectangle means adding its two sides or counting the squares inside it, and the tiling is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: The area of a rectangle is the number of unit squares that tile it, and those squares sit in equal rows. Multiplying the sides counts the rows and the squares in each row at once, which is why the formula is a counting shortcut rather than a separate rule, and it keeps working when a side is fractional.
overview.purpose: The student computes a rectangle's area by rows and columns, explains why multiplication counts them, and extends the argument to fractional sides.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Rectangle fills the main panel with the multiplication line and area readout beneath. On a 390 px frame the side handles keep a 44 px hit target and the grid scrolls rather than shrinking below 12 px squares. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not round the grid to whole squares when a side is fractional, and never show the area before a prediction about the fractional case is committed. A rounded grid would teach that the formula only fits whole numbers.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Tiling a rectangle produces rows that are all the same length, so the total is a repeated addition of that row, which is a multiplication. A fractional side does not break the argument: it produces part squares that themselves combine into whole ones, so the same rows and columns count still gives the total. That is why 3.5 by 4 has an exact area of 14 rather than an approximate one. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): Adding the sides agrees with counting only on the 2 by 2 square, and one agreeing case is not a rule. Breaks: Area found by adding the sides. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A single row is still an array, and multiplying by 1 counts that row exactly once. Breaks: Believing the rows and columns rule needs at least two rows before it can be used. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): The rows and columns rule counts parts of squares in the same breath as whole ones, so it does not stop at whole number sides. Breaks: The formula believed to hold only for whole number sides. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): Multiplying by a length below one unit shrinks the count, so an area can come out smaller than both sides. Breaks: Expecting the answer always to grow, which is what adding the sides would do. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Area is a product, so recovering a side needs the area and one side, never the area by itself. Breaks: Believing the area names the rectangle, so a missing side can be read off the area alone.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on a rectangle of length three and a half and width four, tiled, with the area readout hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether the covered amount will come to a whole number. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets length three and a half, width four. Never count and never state the area at this call. Call 2. Count the rectangle by rows so a whole row lights at a time and the multiplication line is written as the count climbs. Point at the row band and then at the multiplication line. Targets the row route with four rows. Read the total from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Keep the same rectangle and combine the part squares along the fractional edge, then say what the exact area is. Point at the part squares and then at the area readout. Targets length three and a half, width four, part squares combined. Read the exact area from getState().truth.

observationsAndConclusions.why: A rectangle is built from equal rows, so lengthening one side repeats the other side once more
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Dragging one side longer adds a whole column of squares at a time and the area jumps by the other side
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The area depends on both sides at once, which is what multiplying them records

observationsAndConclusions.why: The sum measures how far it is around a piece of the boundary while the count measures how much surface is inside
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The sum of the two sides and the count of the squares part company as soon as the rectangle is not small
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Area and boundary length are different measurements, so no rule turns one into the other

observationsAndConclusions.why: Two halves of a unit square make one unit square, so nothing is lost by the side being fractional
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Halving a side leaves half squares along one edge, and those halves pair up into whole squares
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The rows and columns argument does not need whole number sides, so the formula is exact for fractional sides too

media.description: A rectangle lies on squared paper, seen from directly above, with its unit squares ruled inside it in a lighter line than its own boundary and its length and breadth labelled OUTSIDE it, centred against the midpoint of each side and carrying their unit. Both sides are dragged in half units and the tiling rebuilds square by square, so the area is seen to depend on both sides at once; along a fractional edge the part squares are drawn at their TRUE fraction and are never rounded to whole ones. The counting route is the student's choice and is recorded rather than timed: tapping marks one square at a time, counting by rows lights a whole row and lifts the running total by the row length so the multiplication is written as it emerges, and the third route reads length × breadth straight off the two labels. Where a side is a whole number of halves the part squares PAIR: a dashed completed square is drawn beside the rectangle and a ghost copy of each half slides into it, so 3.5 × 4 reads as exactly 14 square units rather than about 14, and a rectangle whose sides are both under one unit is drawn INSIDE its own unit square, subdivided at its own denominators, so six of twelve cells can be counted. The l + b misconception is made to fail on the picture rather than in a caption: the sum lights only 7 of the 12 drawn squares and the remaining five are hatched and left blank. Hiding the grid leaves the two labelled sides alone and the tiling can be brought back at any moment, so the scaffold fades without being lost. In Practice the quantity the item asks for reads ? on its label, in the multiplication line and in the emitted payload alike, until the attempt is in.

concept.notation: Area is measured in square units. A rectangle of length l and width w holds w rows of l squares, which is why its area is l times w.
concept.statement: The area of a rectangle is the number of unit squares that tile it, and those squares sit in equal rows. Multiplying the sides counts the rows and the squares in each row at once, which is why the formula is a counting shortcut rather than a separate rule, and it keeps working when a side is fractional.
misconceptions: Area found by adding the sides.
The formula believed to hold only for whole number sides.
concept.why_it_is_true: Tiling a rectangle produces rows that are all the same length, so the total is a repeated addition of that row, which is a multiplication. A fractional side does not break the argument: it produces part squares that themselves combine into whole ones, so the same rows and columns count still gives the total. That is why 3.5 by 4 has an exact area of 14 rather than an approximate one.
worked_numbers: A 3 by 4 rectangle holds 4 rows of 3 squares, so 12 square units.
A 3.5 by 4 rectangle holds 4 rows of three and a half squares, so 14 square units exactly.
A 3.5 by 4.5 rectangle has area fifteen and three quarters, which the part squares combine to show.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Part squares are drawn at their true size and combined into whole ones, so the total is exact rather than counted as whole squares.
The corner part square is drawn as a fraction of a fraction, which is where the multiplication of the two fractional parts becomes visible.
A single row is shown and the tool names the area as equal to the other side numerically while keeping the square units.

steps: Predict: a 3.5 by 4 rectangle is drawn with the area HIDDEN. The class commits to whether the area will be a whole number, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.

Fractions: a side becomes fractional, the part squares appear and the same rows and columns argument still gives the total.

normal.shows: The rectangle, the grid toggle, the counting controls, the area readout, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: A 3 by 4 tiled rectangle with both sides free to drag in half units.
play_modes: AGREEING CASE: find every rectangle where adding the sides gives the same number as counting the squares, and say how short the list is.
UNDER BOTH SIDES: build a rectangle whose area is smaller than each of its two sides, then say what the sides have in common.
SAME AREA, NEW SHAPE: fix the area at 24 square units and find every whole sided rectangle that covers it.
GRID OFF: hide the grid, predict an area from the two side readouts, then bring the grid back to check.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example counting by ones when a child asks to before switching to rows.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

mathematical_facts: The area of a rectangle is the number of unit squares that tile it, so it is measured in square units

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the count itself the definition. The squares are marked off one at a time, so the class hears 'twelve squares' before it hears any rule, and the area read-out lands as the name for a count they have just watched being made rather than as the output of a formula.

Beat 2 is the whole argument and the whole misconception in one screen. The rows light one at a time and the running total climbs 3, 6, 9, 12, which is where multiplication is FELT as counting equal groups. Then the sum is tried on the same picture: 3 + 4 lights seven squares warm and the other five are hatched and left standing. Do not say the sum is wrong before those five squares are visible — the point is that the class sees what the sum failed to count.

Beat 3 carries the rule to its useful edge. The breadth is unchanged and the length becomes 3.5, so each of the four rows now ends in a half square. The four halves slide out into two dashed squares beside the rectangle and the total is 14 EXACTLY. Insist on the word exactly, and never say about: this is the beat that decides whether the student believes the formula stops at whole numbers.

Hide the grid and work the same rectangle from its two labels alone. 9. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: Rows of Tiles Fill the Floor
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the area of a rectangle. Students know that area is a tile count. The film must not state the formula and must not give the total.
media.description: A rectangular floor is laid tile by tile, one neat row at a time, and a counter ticks upward. Just before the last row is placed the tiling freezes.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find the area of a rectangle as length times width, and see the diagonal split it in two. Key teaching points: 1) Each row holds as many tiles as the length. 2) There are as many rows as the width. 3) So the total is the length multiplied by the width. 4) A diagonal cuts the rectangle into two triangles of equal area. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often add the length and the width. 2) Students often count tiles individually when the rows are obvious. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of frozen, one row short: ask how many tiles are in one row. 0:25, just before the open question: ask how many rows there will be. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the total will be. After viewing, ask what a diagonal would do to the floor.

topics.summary: The area of a rectangle is the count of unit squares filling it, which is length times width. A diagonal cuts the rectangle into two equal triangles, so each triangle is half of length times width.

content.text:
We measure the area of a region by finding the number of unit squares whose area together equals that of the given region. A unit square is a square of side one unit, so a square of side 1 cm when the unit is the centimetre.

The count need not be a whole number. A region that takes two and a half unit squares to fill has an area of two and a half square units, so the number of unit squares may be a fraction.

Areas are written in square units. A rectangle holding 28 unit squares of side 1 cm has area 28 sq. cm, also written 28 cm squared. Naming the unit is part of the answer, since the same region measures a different number of square metres than square centimetres.

concepts.concept_name: Area, the unit square and square units - the definition

content.text: A rectangle can be filled exactly by rows of unit squares. There are as many rows as the width, and each row holds as many squares as the length. So the total number of unit squares, which is the area, is length multiplied by width. This also means the rectangle with the single longest side is not always the one that covers more surface. To compare two rectangles fairly you compare the products length times width, not just one side.

concepts.concept_name: Area of a rectangle is length times width - free play

content.text: A diagonal of a rectangle joins two opposite corners and cuts the rectangle into two triangles. These two triangles are exactly the same shape and size, so they cover the same number of unit squares. That makes each triangle exactly half of the rectangle. So the area of one such triangle is one half of length times width. For example, a 12 by 7 rectangle has area 84, and each triangle from its diagonal is 42.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Rectangles, squares and the meaning of area
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that the area of a region is the number of unit squares needed to cover it, that a unit square has side one unit, and that the count may be a fraction and is written in square units. They will find the area of a given figure drawn on a unit grid and write it with the correct unit.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Rectangles, squares and the meaning of area
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the rows of unit squares filling a rectangle add up to through observation and reasoning, and determine that a rectangle holds as many rows as its width with as many squares in each row as its length, so its area is length multiplied by width. They will explain that a 9 by 5 rectangle covers 45 unit squares, and that the rectangle covering more surface is found by comparing the products, since 5 by 4 covers 20 while the longer 8 by 1 covers only 8.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Rectangles, squares and the meaning of area
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a diagonal does to a rectangle through observation and reasoning, and determine that it joins two opposite corners and cuts the rectangle into two triangles of exactly the same shape and size, so each triangle covers half of the rectangle. They will explain that a 12 by 7 rectangle covers 84 unit squares, so each triangle from its diagonal covers 42, which is one half of the length times the width.

segments.summary: What area really measures: the count of unit squares a region covers. Reshaping preserves area, a rectangle's area is length times width, and perimeter cannot stand in for area.

media.title: Same Fence, Different Field
media.context: This hook opens the topic on why perimeter cannot measure area. Students know the rectangle formula. The film must not compute either area and must not state the conclusion.
media.description: Two farmers use fences of exactly the same length and yet one field grows far more wheat than the other. The boundaries match to the metre, so how can the surface inside differ so much?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: See that the perimeter of a figure does not determine its area. Key teaching points: 1) Two rectangles can share a perimeter and differ in area. 2) A long thin rectangle wastes its perimeter. 3) The nearer to a square, the larger the area for a fixed perimeter. 4) Perimeter and area measure different things. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume equal perimeters give equal areas. 2) Students often quote a perimeter when asked for an area. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of so how can it differ?: ask which field the class would rent. 0:25, just before the open question: ask how many tiles each field would need. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what perimeter measures. After viewing, ask which shape uses a fence best.

    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the two fences: exactly the same length, a hundred metres each
    the first field: forty five by five
    the second: twenty five by twenty five
    what happens: one field grows far more wheat than the other
    the puzzle: the boundaries match to the metre
    withheld: both areas, and the conclusion

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 35 seconds across 3 scenes.

    Scene 1. Matching to the metre
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 1.8 s  Create(s1_fig0) over 1.2 s, lag_ratio 0.3, to draw figure 1 side by side.
      at 3.8 s  Write(s1_fig0labels) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to label figure 1.
      at 5.5 s  Create(s1_fig1) over 1.2 s, lag_ratio 0.3, to draw figure 2 side by side.
      at 7.4 s  Write(s1_fig1labels) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to label figure 2.
      at 9.1 s  FadeIn(s1_fignote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.7 s  FadeOut(s1_fig0, s1_fig0labels, s1_fig1, s1_fig1labels, s1_fignote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Two farmers use fences of exactly the same length as each other, and yet one of their fields grows far more wheat than the other one does."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. So how can it differ?
      Duration: 13 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.3 s  FadeIn(s2_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 4.5 s  Indicate(s2_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 6.5 s  FadeIn(s2_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 9.1 s  FadeIn(s2_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 11.2 s  FadeOut(s2_sub, s2_lines, s2_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "The boundaries match each other right down to the metre, so how on earth can the surface inside them differ by so much? Nobody moved a fence post anywhere."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. The open question
      Duration: 10 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s3_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 3.3 s  Create(s3_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 5.2 s  FadeIn(s3_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 7.3 s  Circumscribe(s3_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "And nobody bought any extra land either. So why does the same fence enclose such different amounts? Try the Perimeter and Area Grid Builder."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS

    No revealing of the rule, formula or answer anywhere in this hook.
    No worked solution, no general statement of the method.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.

    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.

    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.

media.title: Area Perimeter Contrast
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Mensuration, opening the chapter's area work by pulling area apart from perimeter before any formula is derived. The class already knows A = l × b and P = 2(l + b) from Class 7 and counts unit squares on squared paper; neither is re-derived here. NCERT's own vocabulary is kept: length and BREADTH, 'square units' against 'units', and P = 2(l + b) rather than 2l + 2b, so the half-perimeter (l + b) is a named intermediate the student computes — every worked line in this tool reads sum, then double.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's shapes, the full solution set and the extremal case.
whatYouLearned: Area is counted in square units and perimeter is measured in units, so they are never one number
Two shapes can cover the same amount and need very different lengths of boundary
Two shapes can need the same boundary and cover very different amounts
The square is the extreme member of both families, which is a statement about rectangles and not a rule about all shapes

overview.goal: The student finds shapes with equal area and different perimeter, and the reverse, and states that the two quantities do not determine each other.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying one rectangle on squared paper, its inside shaded square by square and its boundary drawn as a thick cord, with a collecting strip along the foot of the panel. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class claims that two shapes covering the same amount must also need the same length of fencing, and a gallery of shapes is collected to test it.
overview.concept: Area and perimeter are independent measurements of a shape. Rectangles with the same area can have very different perimeters, and rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas, so neither quantity determines the other.
overview.purpose: The student finds shapes with equal area and different perimeter, and the reverse, and states that the two quantities do not determine each other.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Grid fills the main panel with the readouts beside it and the gallery strip along the bottom. On a 390 px frame each side handle keeps a 44 px hit target and the gallery scrolls. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not draw area and perimeter with the same visual cue, and never show them in a shared readout without units. A single combined number would rebuild the very coupling the tool exists to break.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. For a fixed area the sides run through every factor pair, and a long thin pair has a much larger boundary than a squarish pair even though both cover the same number of squares. For a fixed perimeter the sides trade against each other, and the product they make is largest when they are equal. Each family is a set of counterexamples to the coupling belief, and the student generates them rather than being told they exist. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on a rectangle four across and six up with both readouts showing in their own units, and ask the class to say out loud whether two shapes that cover the same amount must need the same length of boundary. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets width four, height six, nothing locked. Never sweep a family before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Lock the covering and sweep the family so the sides run through every whole number pair, and let each shape drop into the gallery with both of its measurements. Point at the boundary readout while the shaded count stays still. Targets the covering locked at the opening shape. Read both readouts from getState().truth. Call 3. Lock the boundary instead and sweep again, so the covering rises to its peak at the squarest member and falls away. Point at the extremal card in the gallery. Targets the boundary locked at the opening shape. Name which member covers most and read its numbers from the tool's own readouts.

whatYouLearned: Area is counted in square units and perimeter is measured in units, so they are never one number
Two shapes can cover the same amount and need very different lengths of boundary
Two shapes can need the same boundary and cover very different amounts
The square is the extreme member of both families, which is a statement about rectangles and not a rule about all shapes

observationsAndConclusions.why: The same number of squares can be laid out long and thin or squarish, and a long thin arrangement has far more boundary for the same inside
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Locking the covering and stepping through the family leaves the shaded count still while the cord around the outside gets much longer
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Equal area does not force equal perimeter, so one measurement cannot be read off the other

observationsAndConclusions.why: With the boundary fixed the two sides trade against each other, and the number of squares they enclose is largest when they are closest to equal
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Locking the boundary instead makes the covering rise to a peak and fall away again
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Perimeter does not fix area either, so the two quantities are independent measurements of the same shape

observationsAndConclusions.why: One count is of squares inside and the other of units of distance around, so an equal numeral is a coincidence of that shape
observationsAndConclusions.observe: On a four by four rectangle both readouts show the same number and still mean different things
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The units are part of the answer, which is why the two readouts are never merged into one

media.description: A rectangle stands on squared paper and its two measurements are taken by two visibly different processes that never share a cue: the interior is COUNTED as unit squares and drives the area read-out in square units, while the boundary is WALKED as a cord ticked one unit segment at a time and drives the boundary read-out in units. The two plates sit side by side and are never merged. Locking the covering enumerates every whole-sided rectangle of that area and steps through the family while a bar chart builds one bar per member — 36 square units gives 1 by 36, 2 by 18, 3 by 12, 4 by 9 and 6 by 6, with boundaries of 74, 40, 30, 26 and 24 units, so five wildly different bars stand over one unchanging shaded count. Locking the boundary instead trades the two sides against each other and the covering rises to a peak at the squarest member. The consolidating beat is the inversion: a 11 by 1 strip (24 units of boundary, 11 square units) drawn beside a 5 by 5 square (20 units of boundary, 25 square units) at ONE shared unit on ONE baseline, so a LONGER cord is seen wrapping a SMALLER patch. Concept demonstrates in three beats, Learn works the five reviewed checkpoints with the answer already on screen, Practice grades a six-item session drawn from a thirty-item pool on a difficulty ladder, and Free Play lets the student drag either side, lock either quantity, sweep the family and collect counterexamples in a gallery.

Beat 2 locks the area and drags the sides through every factor pair, with the perimeter changing at each. Beat 3 locks the perimeter instead and the area changes, peaking at the squarest rectangle. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSides, lockQuantity, addToGallery and say.

concept.notation: Area is counted in square units and perimeter in units. The two readouts carry their units at all times and are never shown as a single number.
concept.statement: Area and perimeter are independent measurements of a shape. Rectangles with the same area can have very different perimeters, and rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas, so neither quantity determines the other.
prerequisites: adding side lengths around a boundary
misconceptions: Area and perimeter believed to rise and fall together.
The two quantities confused, or given in the same units.
concept.why_it_is_true: For a fixed area the sides run through every factor pair, and a long thin pair has a much larger boundary than a squarish pair even though both cover the same number of squares. For a fixed perimeter the sides trade against each other, and the product they make is largest when they are equal. Each family is a set of counterexamples to the coupling belief, and the student generates them rather than being told they exist.
worked_numbers: Area 36 can be 1 by 36 with perimeter 74, 4 by 9 with perimeter 26, or 6 by 6 with perimeter 24.
Perimeter 24 can be 1 by 11 with area 11, 4 by 8 with area 32, or 6 by 6 with area 36.
The square is the extreme case in both families, largest area for a perimeter and smallest perimeter for an area.

extra: Two garden beds that need the same soil but different lengths of fencing
Two photo frames that use the same beading while one holds a bigger picture
A long thin room and a squarish room of the same floor area, skirted along their walls
Two fields of the same boundary wall, one narrow strip and one nearly square
A ribbon of fixed length made into different rectangles on a table
Two rugs of equal area, one runner shaped and one squarish, edged with braid
A pen for goats rebuilt in a squarer shape with the same hurdles
Two sheets of card of equal area trimmed with tape along their edges
textbook: The family of parallelograms drawn together and asked whether their areas agree and whether their perimeters do
The same family asked which member has the largest boundary and which the smallest
A rectangle and a parallelogram built on side lengths that match, compared for which covers more
The rangoli rectangles compared for powder needed rather than for the border drawn around them
A plot whose boundary path is measured while its covered ground is counted separately

answer_key.worked: Area 36 is given by 1 by 36, 2 by 18, 3 by 12, 4 by 9 and 6 by 6, whose perimeters are 74, 40, 30, 26 and 24, so equal area does not force equal perimeter.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the target: every integer sided solution and the extremal case, both as exact values.
answer_key.precision: Integer factor pairs are enumerated exactly for a locked area, and the units stay distinct in the display and in the ground truth object.
answer_key.ground_truth: solutionsForArea(a) = every integer factor pair. solutionsForPerimeter(p) = every integer side pair. extremalCase(target) = the square or nearest squarish pair.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

steps: 2 times 18 is 36 square units for A.

2 plus 18 is 20, half the way round A.
20 times 2 is 40 units of boundary for A.
6 plus 6 is 12, half the way round B.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to separate the two PROCESSES before either number is discussed. The squares drop in one by one and the cord is walked one unit segment at a time, with a tick at every unit boundary and none at the corners, because counting lattice points instead of segments is the off-by-one that makes a 3 by 1 rectangle read as a boundary of 8. Say 'squares inside' and 'steps round the edge', and say the units every time.

Beat 2 is the refutation, and it has to be watched rather than asserted. The area is held at 36 and the sides run through every factor pair; the shaded count never moves while the boundary bar chart builds 74, 40, 30, 26, 24. A caption saying the two are independent teaches nothing — five bars of wildly different height over one unchanging count is the argument.

Beat 3 inverts rather than merely decouples, which is the only arrangement that kills 'a longer boundary must hold more'. The 11 by 1 strip and the 5 by 5 square are drawn at ONE shared unit on ONE baseline: the strip needs 24 units of cord to hold 11 square units while the square needs only 20 to hold 25. Point at the two cords first and the two shaded regions second.

topics.summary: Perimeter measures the boundary, area measures the enclosed surface, and they move independently. Two regions can share a perimeter yet differ in area, and a longer boundary can even wrap a smaller area.

content.text: Perimeter is the length of the boundary of a region. Area is the count of unit squares the region encloses. These are two different quantities, and one does not decide the other. Two rectangles can have the same perimeter yet very different areas: 8 by 1 and 5 by 4 both have perimeter 18, but their areas are 8 and 20. A region can even have a larger perimeter but a smaller area than another, like a long thin strip. So we cannot use perimeter as a measure of area.

content.text: Perimeter is the length of the boundary of a region. Area is the count of unit squares the region encloses. These are two different quantities, and one does not decide the other. Two rectangles can have the same perimeter yet very different areas: 8 by 1 and 5 by 4 both have perimeter 18, but their areas are 8 and 20. A region can even have a larger perimeter but a smaller area than another, like a long thin strip. So we cannot use perimeter as a measure of area.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Rectangles, squares and the meaning of area
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer whether the boundary length of a region fixes the surface it encloses through observation and reasoning, and determine that perimeter and area are separate quantities where one does not decide the other. They will explain that an 8 by 1 rectangle and a 5 by 4 rectangle both have perimeter 18 yet enclose areas of 8 and 20, and that a long thin strip can carry a larger perimeter while enclosing a smaller area, so boundary length can never measure area.

media.title: Floor Plan Cost Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Mensuration, composite figures. The class has met the area of a rectangle, percentage increase, and adding the areas of parts. This tool carries decomposition into a costed situation with real dimensions, so the covered amount and the distance round the walls are separated at exactly the moment money is attached to the answer. Both NCERT routes are used by name — split-and-add and complete-and-subtract — and neither is presented as 'the' method.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's split, each area, the deduced lengths and the cost.
whatYouLearned: A composite plan is measured by splitting it into rectangles whose areas add
The parts must cover the plan exactly, with no gap and no overlap, or the sum measures nothing
An unmarked wall is fixed by the walls facing it and is deduced, never guessed
Cost is area multiplied by a rate, and a wastage allowance enlarges the area bought

overview.goal: The student computes the area of a composite floor plan and the cost of covering it at a given rate, deducing any unmeasured length from the others.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a floor plan drawn to scale with its walls labelled in metres, and a costing strip laid along the foot of the panel. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A room is to be covered and a quotation has to be produced, but one wall on the plan carries no measurement at all.
overview.concept: A composite plan is covered by splitting it into rectangles whose areas add. The cost of covering it is the total area times the rate, and a wastage allowance increases the area to be bought rather than the price of what is laid. A wall with no dimension printed can be deduced from the others, because the plan's lengths must be consistent.
overview.purpose: The student computes the area of a composite floor plan and the cost of covering it at a given rate, deducing any unmeasured length from the others.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Plan fills the main panel with the costing strip beneath. On a 390 px frame the plan keeps full width, split handles keep a 44 px hit target and the costing strip scrolls. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not accept a split that leaves a gap or an overlap, and never let a guessed dimension stand where the plan fixes it. A tolerated guess would turn a constraint argument into a measurement.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Areas of non overlapping parts add, so any exact split of the plan gives the same total, which is why the split regions must tile it with no gaps or overlaps. Opposite runs of an enclosed plan must agree in total length, so an unprinted wall is fixed by the others rather than free to be estimated. Wastage is material bought and cut away, so it enlarges the quantity purchased, and applying it to the cost afterwards happens to give the same number only when the rate is constant. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item loads its own plan, poses the question, then reveals the split, the areas, the total and the cost together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): Parts of a split add to the whole only when they meet edge to edge and share no ground. Breaks: A split whose parts overlap, so one region is paid for twice. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Wastage is extra covering, so it is added to the area; added to the bill it inflates every charge that covers nothing. Breaks: Wastage applied to the cost instead of to the area. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): What is being bought decides whether the plan is measured round its edge or across its floor. Breaks: Perimeter used where area is needed. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The parts must cover the plan exactly, so the total is forced by the region and not by how it was cut. Breaks: A split whose parts leave a gap, so part of the plan is never paid for. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Rounding a cost is a stated decision about money, never a silent trim of the computed value. Breaks: A cost that does not land on a whole rupee treated as an error to be tidied away.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 shows the plan with the total HIDDEN and asks for a rough estimate in square metres. Beat 2 splits the plan into rooms, computes each area and sums them. Beat 3 applies the rate and then a wastage percentage, applied to the area rather than to the cost. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setPlan, addSplitLine, setRate and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the two room plan with its walls labelled in metres, no split drawn and the total hidden, and ask the class to say out loud roughly how many square metres it covers. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Targets the opening plan, no split. Never draw a split before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Split the plan into its two rooms, take each room's area in turn and let the total form as a sum beneath them. Point at each room label and then at the total. Targets the opening plan split into two rooms. Read every area from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Set the rate for each square metre, read the cost, then add a wastage allowance and point at the area bar extending past the plan. Targets the opening plan, the opening rate, an allowance of eight parts in a hundred. Say which quantity the allowance enlarged, and read both costs from the tool's own readouts.

hunts: DOUBLE PAID: draw a split whose parts overlap, watch the total run high, then repair it with one split line moved.
MISSING WALL: hide a printed length and recover it from the walls facing it before the costing strip will settle.
EDGE OR FLOOR: pick three purchases and sort them into the ones needing the boundary and the ones needing the area.
SAME BILL: find two plans of different shape whose covering costs the same at one rate.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The parts do not overlap and leave nothing out, so they measure the same ground however the lines are drawn
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two different splits of the same plan land on the same total every time
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Any exact split will do, which is why the rule is add the parts rather than split it this particular way

observationsAndConclusions.why: A region left out is never counted and a region covered twice is counted twice, so the sum is not the plan's area at all
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A split that leaves a gap or doubles a strip is refused and the offending region stays shaded
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Exact covering is the condition that makes adding the parts legitimate

observationsAndConclusions.why: Waste is material cut away, so it changes what has to be bought, and the two routes agree only because the rate is the same everywhere on this plan
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Applying the allowance to the covering and applying it to the finished price give the same figure here, and the tool still refuses the second route
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A method that happens to give the right number on one case is not the right method, which shows up as soon as two rates are involved

media.description: A rectilinear floor plan is drawn to scale on a plain working ground with a faint one-metre check grid behind it and every wall run labelled outside the outline, mid-run, carrying its unit. The plan is measured two ways at once and both are on screen: a dashed construction line splits it into rectangles whose areas are written inside them and added, and the enclosing rectangle is drawn dashed over the cut corner so the same total arrives by subtracting instead. The parts are painted in translucent tones that composite, so ground claimed by two parts comes out visibly doubled and is named where it happens, while floor no part claims stays hatched and bare; a pair of bars sharing one unit and one origin then drives the parts total PAST the plan's own bar for an overlap and SHORT of it for a gap, so a faulty split is located rather than merely refused. A block a cut leaves that is not yet a rectangle says so instead of being measured. One wall can be left carrying a visible question mark instead of a length and has to be worked out from the runs facing it; a guess is refused and the two runs that force it light up. A costing strip carries the floor in square metres and, kept visibly separate and differently drawn, the run round the edge in metres, then the rate written as rupees per square metre, the allowance for cuts written additively, the area to buy, any fixed fitting charge and the bill. The allowance extends the buying bar past the plan while the plan itself does not move, and because a fixed fitting charge stays on screen the allowance-on-the-bill route parts company from the correct one by exactly the allowance on that charge. A bill carrying paisa keeps its paisa and prints the whole-rupee rule beside it instead of being trimmed.

scenes.subGoal: Explore the picture with nothing scored and nothing required
scenes.onScreen: The plan, the split tools, the rate and wastage controls, the cost, every control, no score and no question. An editable plan with every dimension shown and the rate free to set.
scenes.animation: Split: the plan divides along the line and the regions separate slightly in tone, so the decomposition is visible as regions rather than lines.

scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Lengths are in metres and areas in square metres. A rate is given in rupees per square metre, so the cost is an area multiplied by a rate.
concept.statement: A composite plan is covered by splitting it into rectangles whose areas add. The cost of covering it is the total area times the rate, and a wastage allowance increases the area to be bought rather than the price of what is laid. A wall with no dimension printed can be deduced from the others, because the plan's lengths must be consistent.
misconceptions: Perimeter used where area is needed.
A missing dimension guessed rather than deduced from the plan.
Wastage applied to the cost instead of to the area.
concept.why_it_is_true: Areas of non overlapping parts add, so any exact split of the plan gives the same total, which is why the split regions must tile it with no gaps or overlaps. Opposite runs of an enclosed plan must agree in total length, so an unprinted wall is fixed by the others rather than free to be estimated. Wastage is material bought and cut away, so it enlarges the quantity purchased, and applying it to the cost afterwards happens to give the same number only when the rate is constant.
worked_numbers: Two rooms of 4 by 3 and 5 by 3 metres total 12 plus 15, so 27 square metres.
At 450 rupees per square metre that is 12,150 rupees.
With 8 percent wastage the area bought is 29.16 square metres, costing 13,122 rupees.

extra: An L shaped verandah tiled at a rate for each square metre
A kitchen counter of two rectangular runs, quoted for stone
A hall with a store cupboard cut out of one corner

A courtyard whose paving is bought with an allowance for breakage
A room whose door recess has to be added on before the covering is bought
A strip of matting quoted per square metre and cut to fit two joined areas
A godown floor split into bays, each measured before the bill is made
textbook: The plot with a cross path through it, and the further measurements needed before the path can be measured
The bent spiral tube whose covering is found by splitting it into straight runs
The straight tube asked for that would cover the same amount as the bent one
The shaded region inside a rectangle, found by taking the pieces away from the whole
The composite figures whose separate given lengths have to be assembled into one total
The classroom and the school estimated in square feet and square metres
The conversion between square inches and square centimetres, and between square metres and square kilometres
Land measured in acres and in the local units used in different parts of the country

answer_key.worked: A plan of 4 by 3 and 5 by 3 metres is 27 square metres, which at 450 rupees per square metre with 8 percent wastage costs 13,122 rupees.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the plan and the rate: each room area, the total, the deduced dimensions and the cost.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational arithmetic for areas, with a stated rounding rule for currency. Deduced dimensions are computed from the plan constraints rather than stored separately.
answer_key.ground_truth: roomAreas(plan) = the exact areas. total(plan) = their sum. deduce(plan, wall) = the length forced by the others. cost(area, rate, wastage) = the rounded amount.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

tool_config.tool_objective: The student computes the area of a composite floor plan and the cost of covering it at a given rate, deducing any unmeasured length from the others.

steps: 9 times 4 is 36 square metres for the bottom band.
6 times 6 is 36 square metres for the left block.
36 plus 36 is 72 square metres, which is what the student wrote.
The two parts sit on top of each other in the bottom left corner, a 6 m by 4 m region.
6 times 4 is 24 square metres counted twice.
72 minus 24 is 48 square metres, which the plan agrees with.
items.answer: The parts overlap in a 6 m by 4 m corner, so 24 square metres was counted twice
items.method: Find the double counted region when two parts of a split share ground
items.question: A plan is 9 m by 6 m with a 3 m by 2 m corner cut away, so it covers 48 square metres. A student splits it into a 9 m by 4 m band along the bottom and a 6 m by 6 m block down the left, and adds them to get 72. Where did the extra come from?

stickers.type_method: Find the double counted region when two parts of a split share ground

items.checkpoint: Parts of a split add to the whole only when they meet edge to edge and share no ground.
items.misconception: A split whose parts overlap, so one region is paid for twice.

steps: One tenth of 40 square metres is 4 square metres of wastage.
40 plus 4 is 44 square metres of tiling to buy.
44 times 55 is 2420 rupees for the tiles.
2420 plus 800 is 3220 rupees for the correct bill.
The student adds one tenth of a total that already carries the fitting charge.
One tenth of 800 rupees is 80 rupees, and that is what the customer is overcharged.
items.answer: 80 rupees too much, because the allowance belongs to the tiling and not to the fitting charge
items.method: Apply an allowance for cuts to the area and compare it with applying it to the bill
items.question: Tiles cost 55 rupees per square metre and the fitter charges a fixed 800 rupees. The floor covers 40 square metres and 10 percent extra tiling is needed for cuts. A student works out the bill and then adds 10 percent to the whole total. What does that cost the customer?

stickers.type_method: Apply an allowance for cuts to the area and compare it with applying it to the bill

items.checkpoint: Wastage is extra covering, so it is added to the area; added to the bill it inflates every charge that covers nothing.
items.misconception: Wastage applied to the cost instead of to the area.

steps: 7 times 5 is 35 square metres of floor for the tiles.
7 plus 5 is 12, half the way round the room.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the two routes agree in public. The class watches the plan split into 15 and 12 and add to 27, then watches the enclosing 30 lose its 3 and land on 27 as well. That agreement is what makes 'any exact split will do' believable instead of asserted, and it is worth pointing at both totals and saying they are the same number.

Beat 2 is the argument for the condition. The same plan is claimed by two parts that share ground: the shared corner comes out visibly darker and the parts bar runs PAST the plan's bar by exactly that corner, while the gap case falls SHORT of the same bar. Overlap one way, gap the other, against one reference — that is what turns 'refused' into 'located'.

Beat 3 keeps the fixed fitting charge on screen on purpose. With only a rate the two wastage routes give the same number and the correct method looks arbitrary; with a fixed charge they part company by exactly the allowance on that charge, and that gap is the whole argument. Read both bills off the tool and name which quantity the allowance enlarged.

media.title: The Path Around the Park
media.context: This hook opens the topic on composite figures. Students know the rectangle formula. The film must not state the subtraction and must not give any area.
media.description: A camera circles a rectangular park ringed by a paved walking path, and the paving is highlighted like a picture frame. How much surface does just the path cover, without measuring it stone by stone?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find the area of a composite figure by adding or subtracting simple regions. Key teaching points: 1) A border is the outer area minus the inner area. 2) A composite figure can be split into shapes you already know. 3) Areas of the parts add to the area of the whole. 4) Rearranging the parts does not change the total. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often subtract the perimeters instead of the areas. 2) Students often forget that the path lies on all four sides. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of not stone by stone: ask what two rectangles the picture holds. 0:23, just before the open question: ask which one has to be taken away. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the outer rectangle measures. After viewing, ask how they would find the grass alone.

topics.summary: Composite areas are found by adding and subtracting rectangles: a border is outer minus inner, a crosspath is two strips minus their overlap, and a bent tube of constant width equals the straight tube of the same length.

content.text: A path or border around a rectangular region is the ring between an outer rectangle and an inner rectangle. Its area is simply the outer area minus the inner area. When a path of a fixed width runs inside all four sides, each side of the inner rectangle is shorter by twice the width, since the path eats into both ends. Because the border area depends only on the two rectangles and not on where they sit, sliding the outer rectangle around a fixed inner region does not change the border area.

content.text: Any composite figure can be broken into rectangles whose areas simply add up. When two strips cross, like a crosspath through a plot, the square where they overlap belongs to both, so adding both strips counts it twice; we subtract one overlap to count it once. Because area is additive and does not change when pieces are rearranged, a bent tube of constant width has exactly the same area as the straight tube of the same width and total length: straightening it keeps every unit square.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what fills the ring between two rectangles through observation and reasoning, and determine that the area of a border equals the outer rectangle's area minus the inner rectangle's area, and that a path of fixed width running inside all four sides shortens each inner side by twice the width. They will explain that a 20 by 14 outer rectangle around a 16 by 10 park leaves a border of 280 minus 160, which is 120 square metres, and that sliding the outer rectangle without resizing leaves this unchanged.

Students will be able to infer what happens when a figure is broken into rectangles and rearranged through observation and reasoning, and determine that composite area is the sum of the rectangle pieces, that a square counted by two crossing strips must be subtracted once, and that rearranging pieces never changes the total. They will explain that an L shaped room of a 10 by 4 rectangle joined to a 6 by 3 rectangle covers 40 plus 18, which is 58 square metres, and that a bent tube of constant width matches the straight tube of equal length.

topics.summary: A triangle fills exactly half the rectangle on its base and perpendicular height, so its area is one half of base times height. The height is always the perpendicular distance, never a slanted side.

content.text: Any triangle fills exactly half of the rectangle built on its base and its perpendicular height. So the area of a triangle is one half of base times height. The height must be the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base line, not a slanted side, which is always longer and would overstate the area. This works for every triangle: for an obtuse triangle the height falls outside the base, and the area comes out as the difference of two right triangles, but the same formula still holds.

This works for every triangle: for an obtuse triangle the height falls outside the base, and the area comes out as the difference of two right triangles, but the same formula still holds.

content.text: A triangle has just one area, but each side can serve as the base with its own perpendicular height. So one half times base times height gives the same number whichever side you choose. This lets you find a missing altitude: write the area from a known base and height, then set it equal to one half times the other base times the unknown height and solve. Because the area stays fixed, a longer base always goes with a shorter height, and a shorter base with a taller height.

overview.concept: A triangle is exactly half the rectangle on the same base and height, so its area is half of base times height. Any triangle with the same base whose apex lies on a fixed parallel line has the same area, however different it looks, because the base and the height are both unchanged.

overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with the area readout beneath. On a 390 px frame the apex and the base ends each keep a 44 px hit target and the parallel line spans the full width. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not let the apex leave the parallel line during a shear, and never hide the height when it falls outside the triangle. A hidden external height would suggest obtuse triangles follow a different rule.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Two copies of a triangle join into a rectangle on the same base and height, so one copy is half of it. The apex sliding along a parallel line keeps its perpendicular distance to the base fixed by construction, and half of base times height depends on nothing else, so the area cannot move. When the apex slides far enough that the foot of the perpendicular leaves the base, the height is measured to the extended base line and the same rule still applies. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on a triangle whose base is eight and whose height is five, with the apex sitting on the dashed rail and the outcome hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether sliding the top corner sideways makes it grow, shrink or stay the same. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets base eight, height five, apex above the middle. Never slide the apex before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Turn a second copy into place so the rectangle on the same base and height is completed, and point at the two equal pieces. Targets base eight, height five, the completing copy shown. Say what fraction of the rectangle one copy is, and read the areas from getState().truth. Call 3. Slide the apex along the rail to the far right so the triangle becomes obtuse and the perpendicular meets the extended base line, and point at the area readout while it stays still. Targets base eight, height five, apex beyond the right end of the base. Read the area from getState().truth, never from this plan.

hunts: SLIDE FOR EVER: drag the apex as far along the dashed line as it will go and say what the area readout does.
OFF THE LINE: leave the dashed line and find the apex positions that double the area.
COLLAPSE: bring the apex down to the base line and say what the readout shows and why.
SLANT TRAP: build a triangle where the slant and the height differ most, and say how far wrong the slant would put you.
