observationsAndConclusions.why: The apex stays the same perpendicular distance from the base line, and half of base times height depends on nothing else
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The triangle deforms through every shape on the rail and the area readout does not flicker
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Shapes that look completely different can have exactly the same area, so appearance is not a measurement

observationsAndConclusions.why: The turned copy fills exactly the part of the rectangle the triangle does not, so the two pieces are equal
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two copies of the triangle lock together into the rectangle on the same base and the same height with nothing left over
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The half in the rule is the undoing of a doubling that can be watched, not a factor to memorise

observationsAndConclusions.why: The height is a distance to the base line rather than a segment inside the figure, and that line can always be extended
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Once the apex slides past the end of the base, the perpendicular meets a line drawn on beyond the base and the area still does not move
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An obtuse triangle needs no separate rule; it is the same rule with the foot of the perpendicular outside the base

media.description: A base AB is drawn heavy on a light unit grid and a triangle stands on it with its top vertex riding a dashed rail parallel to the base. The vertex can be sent anywhere along that rail, including well past either end of the base, and as it travels the triangle visibly reshapes: the two slanted sides stretch and shorten, the dashed perpendicular stays exactly the gap between the two parallels with its square right-angle mark riding along the base and out onto the dashed extension when the foot leaves it, and the area read-out does not move by a single unit. Two live read-outs run side by side while it travels - the slanted side ticking up, the perpendicular height standing still - which is what makes the height-is-a-side error fail on screen rather than in a caption. Trails of every position passed accumulate into a fan of very different-looking triangles standing under one printed area, and a ghost rectangle on the same base and height stays put through the whole journey so the two off-cut pieces are seen trading ground from one side to the other. A second copy of the triangle turns 180 degrees about the midpoint of a side and lands, completing that rectangle exactly, which is where the half in the rule comes from. Raising or lowering the rail moves the area of the WHOLE family at once, which is what separates 'the area depends on the height' from 'the area depends on where the top vertex is'. Concept runs three teaching beats (the vertex travels, two copies make the rectangle, past the end of the base); Learn works the five reviewed checkpoints on their own numbers with the answer already on screen; Practice serves six of a thirty-item pool on a difficulty ladder with a star screen and a review walk; Free Play hands the vertex, the base end, the rail, the trails and the rectangle to the student.

scenes.subGoal: Explore the picture with nothing scored and nothing required
scenes.onScreen: The triangle, the parallel line, the height, the rectangle toggle, every control, no score and no question. A triangle with the apex free to slide anywhere along the parallel line.
scenes.animation: Shear: the triangle deforms continuously as the apex travels, with the area readout visibly still, which is the invariance being felt rather than read.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

concept.notation: The height is the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base line, which may fall outside the triangle. A shear moves the apex along a line parallel to the base, so the height cannot change.
concept.statement: A triangle is exactly half the rectangle on the same base and height, so its area is half of base times height. Any triangle with the same base whose apex lies on a fixed parallel line has the same area, however different it looks, because the base and the height are both unchanged.
misconceptions: The area assumed to change whenever the shape changes.
The height taken as a side rather than as a perpendicular.
Obtuse triangles believed to need a different rule.
concept.why_it_is_true: Two copies of a triangle join into a rectangle on the same base and height, so one copy is half of it. The apex sliding along a parallel line keeps its perpendicular distance to the base fixed by construction, and half of base times height depends on nothing else, so the area cannot move. When the apex slides far enough that the foot of the perpendicular leaves the base, the height is measured to the extended base line and the same rule still applies.
worked_numbers: Base 8 and height 5 give area 20 square units, half of the 40 square unit rectangle.
Sliding the apex from above the middle of the base to far off to one side leaves the area at 20.
In the obtuse case the height 5 is measured to the extended base line, and the area is still 20.

answer_key.worked: A triangle with base 8 and height 5 has area 20 square units, and every triangle on that base with its apex on the same parallel line has the same area.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from base and height, with the external height case flagged in the ground truth where it arises.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational area. The apex is constrained to the parallel line by construction, so the height is fixed rather than recomputed and rounded.
answer_key.ground_truth: area(base, height) = half the exact product. heightIsExternal(apex, base) = whether the foot lies off the base. equalArea(t1, t2) = same base and same height.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

normal.shows: The triangle, the parallel line, the height, the rectangle toggle, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: A triangle with the apex free to slide anywhere along the parallel line.
play_modes: SLIDE FOR EVER: drag the apex as far along the dashed line as it will go and say what the area readout does.
OFF THE LINE: leave the dashed line and find the apex positions that double the area.
COLLAPSE: bring the apex down to the base line and say what the readout shows and why.
SLANT TRAP: build a triangle where the slant and the height differ most, and say how far wrong the slant would put you.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example sliding the apex to the extreme position a child predicts will break it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

mathematical_facts: Two copies of a triangle join into a rectangle on the same base and the same height, so a triangle is half of base times height
The height is the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base line, which is not in general the length of a side
Moving the apex along a line parallel to the base leaves the base and the height unchanged, so the area cannot change
When the foot of the perpendicular falls outside the base, the height is measured to the extended base line and the same rule holds

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class watches the number refuse to move. The vertex travels the whole rail from x = -4 to x = 14 while the perpendicular height read-out stands at 5 and the slanted-side read-out climbs past 14, and the trail it leaves is a fan of triangles that look nothing like one another standing under one printed area. Ask for the prediction OUT LOUD before calling gotoStep(0); it is never rendered on screen.

Beat 2 is where the half comes from, and the top vertex is parked directly above A on purpose. Rotating a copy 180 degrees about the midpoint of a side completes a RECTANGLE only for a right-angled triangle; anywhere else the two copies make a parallelogram, and a parallelogram argument would lean on a result this chapter has not reached. Say out loud that the height happens to run along a side in this one position, so nobody leaves believing that is what a height is.

Beat 3 is the case that looks different and obeys the same rule. The base line grows a dashed extension, the right-angle mark rides out onto it and the area read-out does not flinch. Never hide the height here: hiding it is exactly what convinces a class that obtuse triangles need a rule of their own.

media.instructions_for_student: Two lines run across the screen the same distance apart the whole way — that distance is the height of every triangle you can build here. The base AB sits on the lower line and never changes. Drag the orange tip anywhere along the upper line, even past the ends of the base, and watch the two numbers: one of them refuses to move, and one of them changes with every step you take. Pause somewhere and the triangle leaves a faint ghost behind, so you can build a whole fan of different-looking triangles and read the single area they all share. Use the − and + buttons to make the base longer or shorter, or to move the upper line up and down, and see which of those actually changes the area. Press 'Run the reflection' to find the one tip position that makes the perimeter as small as it can be.

topics.summary: Triangles on a fixed base with the apex anywhere on a parallel line all have the same area, since base and height are both fixed. The perimeter, unlike the area, changes and has a single minimum.

content.text: Take a fixed base and a line parallel to it. Every triangle with that base and its third vertex somewhere on the parallel line has the same area. This is because the area is one half of base times perpendicular height, the base is fixed, and the height is the constant gap between the two parallel lines. So as the apex slides along the parallel line, the triangle changes shape and its perimeter goes up and down, but its area never changes. The perimeter has a single smallest value, found by a mirror-reflection argument, but the area is always the same.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what stays fixed as the apex of a triangle slides along a line parallel to its base through observation and reasoning, and determine that every such triangle keeps the same area, since the base is fixed and the height is the constant gap between the parallels. They will explain that a triangle with base 8 and its apex on a line 5 away covers 20 square units wherever the apex sits, so the shape and perimeter change while the area never does.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving same base between the same parallels means equal area, across different cases.

media.title: Grid Polygon Counter
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Mensuration - the area of any polygon on a squared grid, by splitting it into parts whose areas add and by taking the outside pieces away from an enclosing rectangle (NCERT Ch. 9, 'Area of a General Quadrilateral' and 'Area of a Polygon'). The class has met area, region, enclosed, polygon, diagonal, perpendicular, vertex, congruent, trapezium and square unit; it has NOT met decomposition as a noun of art, bounding box, union, partition, additivity or concave, so the screen says 'split it into parts', 'cut it out of a rectangle' and 'a polygon with a notch cut into it'. The board carries no length unit, so every reading is in SQUARE UNITS spelt out - never cm squared and never units with a raised 2. In Class 5 these students were taught the approximate grid rule (more than half covered counts 1, less than half counts 0, exactly half counts a half); this tool's 45 degree edges make every crossed square EXACTLY half, the one case where the old rule and the exact answer agree, and the tool says 'exactly half, so a half' rather than contradicting what they were taught.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's parts, whether they covered exactly and the exact area.
whatYouLearned: A polygon can be measured by cutting it into parts whose areas add
It can also be measured by taking the outside pieces away from an enclosing rectangle
Both routes must agree, because both measure the same region
A square a sloping edge cuts in half contributes a half, never a whole

overview.goal: The student finds the area of a grid polygon by decomposing it or by subtracting from a bounding rectangle, and justifies the route chosen.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a pegboard, with the polygon strung between pegs and a parts list building down the side of the panel. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A four sided figure with one sloping edge is stretched on the pegboard and two students insist on measuring it in different ways.
overview.concept: The area of a polygon on a grid can be found by cutting it into rectangles and triangles and adding, or by enclosing it in a rectangle and subtracting the pieces outside it. Both routes must give the same total, because both measure the same region.
overview.purpose: The student finds the area of a grid polygon by decomposing it or by subtracting from a bounding rectangle, and justifies the route chosen.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Pegboard fills the main panel with the parts list beneath and both totals side by side. On a 390 px frame every peg keeps a 44 px hit target and the board scrolls rather than shrinking. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not accept a sum from parts that overlap or leave a gap, and never round a half square along a sloping edge to a whole one. A tolerated gap would teach that area is approximately additive.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Area is additive over parts that do not overlap, so any exact cover gives the same total, and subtracting the outside pieces from an enclosing rectangle is the same statement rearranged. That is why two independent routes must agree: they are two decompositions of the same region. Where they disagree, the parts have failed to cover exactly, which the tool checks geometrically rather than by comparing totals. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A decomposition counts the region once only when no square lies in two parts. Breaks: A decomposition whose parts overlap, so a region is counted twice. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Subtracting from a bounding rectangle works only when every piece between the rectangle and the outline is taken off. Breaks: The bounding rectangle method applied without subtracting every corner. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Area belongs to the region, so two correct routes cannot disagree; a disagreement is a fault to be found. Breaks: Treating the answer as depending on the route chosen rather than on the region. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A square the outline crosses is not a square inside, so a cut square carries only the part that lies within. Breaks: Part squares along a sloping edge counted as whole ones. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The route changes only the risk of error, never the area, which the region has already fixed. Breaks: Believing the route chosen changes the answer rather than only the chance of a mistake.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the four sided figure strung on the pegboard with one sloping edge and the area hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether they would split it up or cut it out of a rectangle. Commit the class choice on the prediction pad. Targets the opening polygon, the decomposition route offered. Never draw a split before the choice is committed. Call 2. Draw the split so the figure separates into a rectangle and a corner piece, measure each part in turn and let the running total build in the parts list. Point at each part label and then at the total. Targets the opening polygon split into two parts. Read every part area from getState().truth. Call 3. Switch to the other route, draw the enclosing rectangle, take the corner pieces away and let the two totals stand side by side. Point at the two totals as they lock together. Targets the opening polygon, both routes complete. Read both totals from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan.

hunts: COUNT IT TWICE: draw a split whose parts cross, read the inflated total, then find the patch that caused it.
TWO ROUTES: measure one polygon by decomposing and by subtracting, and say which took fewer readings.
HALF SQUARES: build an outline whose sloping edge cuts as many squares as you can, then bracket its area.
DEEP NOTCH: cut a notch so far in that the bounding rectangle route needs the fewest pieces, and say why.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Both routes measure the same region, one by adding the parts inside and one by taking the outside away from the whole
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The two routes land on the same total on every figure that is covered exactly
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Agreement between two independent routes is evidence, which is why the tool asks for both rather than one

observationsAndConclusions.why: The strip inside both parts is counted twice, so the total is larger than the region and measures no figure at all
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A pair of parts that overlap shades in a warning tone and the sum is refused
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Covering exactly, with no gap and no overlap, is the condition that makes adding the parts legal

observationsAndConclusions.why: The edge divides the square it crosses, so the part inside is a fraction of it rather than the whole of it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Where the sloping edge crosses a square it leaves a triangle, and two such triangles make one square
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Counting a crossed square as a whole one inflates the answer, which is why the halves are counted as halves

media.description: A pegboard of unit squares carries an outline strung between whole-number pegs, and the same outline is measured two ways at once. Peg-to-peg cut lines split the region into parts and each part carries its own area on the board, so the sum is read off named pieces rather than asserted; a dashed enclosing rectangle can be drawn around the same outline and the pieces between the two are lifted off one at a time, so the subtraction route runs on the identical figure. Every region in the tool is held as a set of QUARTER CELLS, so an overlap, a gap or an unsubtracted piece is a SET OF SQUARES the tool can shade on the board - never a difference of two totals - and a decomposition that does not cover exactly is refused geometrically with the offending squares lit. A 45 degree edge cuts each square it crosses into exactly two halves, which is where the Class 5 habit of rounding a crossed square up to a whole one is made to fail: the tool counts whole squares, cut squares and every touched square side by side and prints the staircase the whole-square count claims. Concept runs three teaching beats (split and add, cut it out of a rectangle, a cut square is half a square); Learn works the five reviewed checkpoints with the answer already on screen; Practice serves six of a thirty-item pool on a difficulty ladder with a star screen and a review walk; Free Play hands the student the pegboard, the four tools and the two routes.

concept.notation: Area is counted in grid squares. A decomposition is a set of parts that covers the polygon with no gaps and no overlaps; a subtraction is a bounding rectangle minus the corner pieces.
concept.statement: The area of a polygon on a grid can be found by cutting it into rectangles and triangles and adding, or by enclosing it in a rectangle and subtracting the pieces outside it. Both routes must give the same total, because both measure the same region.
misconceptions: Part squares along a sloping edge counted as whole ones.
A decomposition whose parts overlap, so a region is counted twice.
The bounding rectangle method applied without subtracting every corner.
concept.why_it_is_true: Area is additive over parts that do not overlap, so any exact cover gives the same total, and subtracting the outside pieces from an enclosing rectangle is the same statement rearranged. That is why two independent routes must agree: they are two decompositions of the same region. Where they disagree, the parts have failed to cover exactly, which the tool checks geometrically rather than by comparing totals.
worked_numbers: A polygon with vertices at (0,0), (4,0), (4,3) and (1,5) splits into a 4 by 3 rectangle and a triangle of base 3 and height 2, so 12 plus 3, which is 15.
By subtraction: the 4 by 5 bounding rectangle is 20, minus a triangle of 3 and a rectangle of 2, which is 15.
A sloping edge crossing squares diagonally contributes half squares, not whole ones.

answer_key.worked: The polygon with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (4,3) and (1,5) has area 15 square units by decomposition and 15 by subtraction from its bounding rectangle.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the vertex list by the shoelace formula, which is exact on integer coordinates.
answer_key.precision: Ground truth area by the shoelace formula on integer coordinates, exact. The student's decomposition is checked by comparing the union of the parts against the polygon geometrically.
answer_key.ground_truth: shoelace(vertices) = the exact area. coversExactly(parts, polygon) = whether the union matches with no gap or overlap. boundingRectangle(vertices) = the enclosing rectangle and its corner pieces.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The overlap is shaded and the sum is refused, since a region counted twice is not a decomposition.
The gap is shaded and named, rather than the total being accepted as close enough.

edge_cases.case: A sloping edge cutting squares in half
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Half squares are counted as halves, and the tool states the exact contribution rather than rounding to whole squares.
The subtraction route needs more than one corner piece, which the tool requires rather than accepting a single subtraction.
The tool locates the part that fails to cover exactly, since two correct routes cannot differ.
